rv.q: Hall's script takes so much time easing into the family's traditions and lore that the drama in 'The Blood Quilt' is slow to get any traction.
The mounting frustration of The Blood Quilt arises from its increasingly blatant pile-up of contrivance.
The Blood Quilt is a hearty and heartfelt family drama set in a mostly overlooked corner of America. Like the culture it depicts, you need to see it before it is gone.

Director Lileana Blain-Cruz traverses the often fractious but ultimately loving relationships between the women with compassion and humor, as Ms. Hall emphasizes the role their heritage plays in binding them to each other, and to their ancestors.
With its relentlessly watchable performances, The Blood Quilt is a well-crafted addition to the fruitful genre of the homecoming play.
The good word is that she has succeeded at writing a drama that will last, that will endure.

Newhouse Theater at Lincoln Center, the thread is a literal one, as four grown daughters gather together following the death of their mother to carry out their long-established ritual of a sewing circle. As you enter the theater, you will get a good sense of the setting as laid out in Adam Rigg's design.
But the rich quality of her dialogue and the cast's full embrace of the family's dynamics makes it worth checking out The Blood Quilt's intricate stitching.
It’s well worth seeing for the compelling story, the vibrant characters, the deep history, and the sensational conclusion (featuring water, of course, the play’s chief symbol, that flows throughout).
Lileana Blain-Cruz directs her tight-knit ensemble with a steady hand so that even the most volatile moments never dip into histrionics or melodrama.
The Blood Quilt stitched storylines that gripped me emotionally until the play's end.
